_comment: THE INTENDED BOOT CONFIGURATION FOR BOTH NODES. The live file is /var/tmp/vllm-kv-flags/flags.json, which is per-node and NOT in git -- so this committed copy is the reviewable, recoverable source and local-ops/flags-apply.sh is what installs it. Keep them in step.
_why_not_in_flags_py_defaults: flags.py's DEFAULTS carry a deliberate invariant, stated in its own header: an EMPTY FLAGS FILE BEHAVES EXACTLY AS TODAY, every new mechanism off, so a deploy is a no-op until somebody writes a flag. Turning the disk tier on there would break that. The code defaults stay inert; this file is the configuration. The one exception is load_inflight_max, which is a SAFETY bound and belongs in the code default precisely because inert-by-default is correct for it.
_why_journal: THE PRESENCE JOURNAL IS ON, AND IT CLOSES A MEASURED DATA-LOSS WINDOW. The manifest is O(index) to persist O(changes) -- 772,561 keys rewritten for the ~71 a response adds -- and under live store load it saturates: manifest_writes 109 against manifest_skipped_busy 462, so 81% of flush attempts were refused as already busy. flush_manifest is only ever CALLED from complete_store, so a refused flush is never retried once stores stop. Measured on the live engine 2026-10-11 with the store paused since 14:06: presence.json held 868,376 keys while memory held 873,551 -- 5,175 keys / ~3.7 GB of files that no future boot could name. A clean shutdown forces a flush and closes that window; an unclean kill does not, and an unclean kill (Xid, NCCL abort, SIGKILL) is how this process normally ends. With the journal on, every presence edge is one append and the snapshot becomes the COMPACTION of a journal rather than the durability mechanism. The bounds are compaction triggers: either trips it, and a zero or negative value disables that half rather than meaning always. journal_fsync stays at its code default of OFF: flush() already survives the PROCESS dying, which is the failure being prevented; fsync only adds cover for machine power loss at a sync per store round on the scheduler thread. NOTE IT DOES NOT SHRINK THE 256s BOOT WALK -- every key is still stat'ed because offloading/worker.py:273 asserts on a failed load, which is independent of the index file format.
_why_store_paused: THE STORE IS LIVE AGAIN AS OF 2026-10-11, AND THE JOURNAL IS WHY. It was paused because the store path stalled the stream by ~1.1s (test-meter.sh section 1: max inter-event gap 1.137s against a 0.102s baseline, A/B/A 1.109 / 0.111 / 1.067). The cause was the MANIFEST FLUSH, not the pump: O(index) to persist O(changes), 772,561 keys rewritten for the ~71 a response adds. Moving it off the engine core's thread removed the stall but left a 0.153s snapshot on the caller's thread and an 81% refusal rate (manifest_writes 109 against manifest_skipped_busy 462). The presence journal removes both: every presence edge is one append and the snapshot becomes a compaction. MEASURED ON THE LAN, store live and journal on, A/B/A: 0.135 live / 0.135 PAUSED CONTROL / 0.099 live, against the 0.102s baseline -- indistinguishable, with manifest_writes 0 and skipped_busy 0 across 230 keys stored, 173 appends and 19.5 KB of journal while the 70.9 MB presence.json was never rewritten. Earlier verification of the off-thread fix alone was done over the WAN with a ~0.6s floor that could hide the residual; this one is not. AND THE DURABILITY HALF IS WHY IT MATTERED MORE THAN LATENCY: the restart on 2026-10-11 LOST 5,175 keys / 3.69 GB from the index across a deliberate, clean `docker compose down` -- presence.json held 868,376 while memory held 873,551, and the boot loaded exactly 868,376. Those files are on disk and no future boot can name them. A clean shutdown does NOT close that window, which an earlier note here wrongly assumed; there is no clean path that saves them, so the journal is the only mechanism. If the stream ever regresses, the knob to try first is journal_enabled, not disk_store_paused.
_why_load_ops_max: THE XID 32 EXPERIMENT, 2026-10-14. Every ledgered Xid 32 that day (12:12, 12:43, 13:03, 13:44 CEST) fell on a GROUP-0 load at exactly the op cap: 33 blocks x 62 refs = 2,046 descriptors in one copy call. The 13:44 one was ALONE on the GPU (gpu_loads=0, gpu_stores=0), not writing in-step blocks (in_step=0), with 0 overlaps -- after kvmgr v0.4.1 had removed load bursts. No other group's loads reach the cap in practice. Halved to 1024 so group-0 loads are 16 blocks (992 ops). If the Xids stop under normal traffic the trigger is the copy size; if they continue it is not. Code default stays 2048 until this is measured.
